common_name: Cherokee Crape Myrtle (Red-Flowered Dwarf-to-Medium Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cherokee is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's earlier Native American tribe-named crape myrtle releases, a Lagerstroemia indica selection predating the mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids like Natchez.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Cherokee is a bright red-flowering crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's early tribe-named breeding series, producing dense clusters of vivid red crepe-textured flowers through the heat of summer on a dwarf-to-medium multi-stemmed shrub. Being a straight Lagerstroemia indica selection rather than one of the later indica x fauriei hybrids, it carries more susceptibility to powdery mildew than mildew-resistant selections like Natchez or Tuscarora, so give it full sun and good air circulation to minimize disease pressure. Its more compact size compared to the largest crape myrtle cultivars makes it a fit for smaller landscapes or foundation plantings where a full-size tree form would be too large. As with all crape myrtles, never top or hard-prune the main framework — a practice sometimes called 'crepe murder' — since it ruins the natural vase-shaped form permanently; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Miami Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Cinnamon-Bark Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Miami is a U.S. National Arboretum indica x fauriei hybrid released in 1979, growing into a tall, mildew-resistant tree with striking exfoliating bark.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Miami is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei hybrid releases, combining the flower power of common crape myrtle with the disease resistance and exceptional bark of Lagerstroemia fauriei. It produces abundant dark-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a tall, upright tree, and as it matures the outer bark exfoliates to reveal smooth, rich cinnamon-brown inner bark that becomes a major ornamental feature through fall and winter after the leaves drop. Its strong resistance to powdery mildew, the primary disease problem of straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, makes it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South summers. Its eventual height puts it among the larger crape myrtle selections, better suited to a specimen planting or street tree role than a small foundation bed. Never top or hard-prune the main framework; prune selectively in late winter only to remove crossing or crowded growth.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Yuma Crape Myrtle (Lavender-Flowered Mildew-Resistant Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yuma is a U.S. National Arboretum indica x fauriei hybrid, part of the same tribe-named mildew-resistant breeding program that produced Natchez and Muskogee.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Yuma is a medium-sized crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei breeding program, producing generous clusters of soft lavender flowers through the summer on a well-branched, upright tree. Like its better-known siblings such as Natchez and Muskogee, it carries strong resistance to powdery mildew, the primary disease that plagues straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in humid climates, along with good fall foliage color and attractive bark as the tree matures. Its medium mature size makes it a versatile choice for a specimen tree in a moderate-size yard where the largest crape myrtles would eventually overwhelm the space. Never top or hard-prune the main framework, since this permanently disfigures the natural form; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Pecos Crape Myrtle (Compact Pink Mildew-Resistant Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pecos is a compact U.S. National Arboretum indica x fauriei hybrid bred for smaller landscapes and foundation plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pecos is one of the more compact selections from the U.S. National Arboretum's mildew-resistant Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei breeding program, staying small enough for foundation plantings, smaller landscapes, and large containers where full-size crape myrtles would quickly outgrow the space. It produces abundant clear-pink flower clusters through summer on a dense, well-branched dwarf-to-medium shrub, along with the strong powdery mildew resistance characteristic of the fauriei-hybrid crape myrtles. Its small mature size means it needs little to no size-control pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter — never top or hard-prune crape myrtles, since this ruins the naturally graceful branching form. A dependable, low-maintenance choice for a smaller garden that still wants the long summer bloom crape myrtles are known for.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Seminole Crape Myrtle (Medium Pink Early-Series Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seminole is one of the U.S. National Arboretum's earlier Native American tribe-named crape myrtle releases, a Lagerstroemia indica selection predating the mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Seminole is a medium-pink flowering crape myrtle from the U.S. National Arboretum's early tribe-named breeding series, one of the longest-established selections still found in Southern landscapes, producing abundant crepe-textured flower clusters through the heat of summer on a dense, multi-stemmed shrub. As a straight Lagerstroemia indica cultivar rather than one of the later, more mildew-resistant indica x fauriei hybrids, it benefits from full sun and good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew pressure in humid climates. Its long track record and moderate size make it a familiar, dependable choice for a summer-flowering hedge, screen, or specimen shrub. Never top or hard-prune the main framework; prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or crowded twiggy growth and maintain the natural vase-shaped form.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Toto Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Award-Winning Rudbeckia Series)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Toto was the first genuinely compact black-eyed susan series bred for bedding and container use, and won the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost, or transplant started seedlings, into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Toto is a landmark black-eyed susan series bred to bring the familiar large, showy, dark-centered gold daisy flowers of Rudbeckia hirta down onto a genuinely compact, uniform 12-14 inch plant, well suited to bedding lines, mass plantings, and containers where the taller straight species would be out of scale. It flowers heavily and continuously from summer through frost, holding up well to Gulf South heat and humidity, and was recognized with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its garden performance. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom, though the plant remains attractive and productive with minimal grooming. Rudbeckia hirta is typically grown as an annual or short-lived biennial/perennial; it often self-sows where happy, giving a return show the following year.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Award of Garden Merit

common_name: Blue River II Hardy Hibiscus (Large White Dinner-Plate Hibiscus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost, or plant nursery divisions, in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Blue River II is a Dr. Harold Winters hybrid bred for enormous pure-white flowers on a cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges late in spring.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Blue River II is a classic hardy hibiscus hybrid bred by Dr. Harold Winters, producing enormous, pure-white, dinner-plate-size flowers — often 8 to 10 inches across, among the largest flowers of any hardy garden perennial — over a mounding plant with maple-like green foliage. Unlike tropical hibiscus, it is fully cold-hardy and dies back completely to the ground each winter, re-emerging quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown before new growth appears. It thrives in reliably moist to wet soil and tolerates boggy conditions better than most perennials, making it a strong choice for a rain garden or pond margin as well as a well-watered border. Individual flowers last only a day, but a mature plant produces a long, heavy succession of blooms from mid- to late summer. Cut the dead stalks to the ground in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Moy Grande Hardy Hibiscus (Giant Cherry-Red Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant nursery divisions or container plants after last frost in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Moy Grande, bred by Ying Doon Moy at the San Antonio Botanical Center from a cross of Hibiscus moscheutos and H. grandiflorus, produces some of the largest flowers of any garden hibiscus.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, giving it plenty of room since it grows into one of the largest hardy hibiscus available. Moy Grande, bred in San Antonio from a cross between the eastern swamp mallow Hibiscus moscheutos and the southern rose mallow H. grandiflorus, produces truly enormous deep cherry-pink-to-red flowers — commonly 10 to 12 inches across, among the largest of any perennial flower — on a tall, robust plant with soft, felted gray-green foliage. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and is notably slow to emerge in spring, so avoid disturbing the crown before new shoots appear. It needs consistently moist to wet soil and heavy feeding to fuel its rapid summer growth and giant flowers, making it well suited to a rain garden, pond margin, or well-irrigated border. Cut dead stalks to the ground in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: San Antonio Botanical Garden — Moy Grande introduction

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tama-no-Ura was discovered growing wild on the Gotō Islands of Nagasaki, Japan, in 1947 and is prized for its clean white-edged red flowers, a distinctive natural pattern that seldom reverts.

directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and hot midday sun; Tama-no-Ura is a celebrated Japanese camellia cultivar discovered growing wild on the Gotō Islands off Nagasaki in 1947, bearing single, rich red flowers cleanly edged in white — a naturally occurring bicolor pattern that, unlike many mottled or streaked camellias, holds true and rarely reverts to solid color. The glossy, deep-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, and the plant blooms in winter into early spring, when few other shrubs are in flower. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it needs consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soil and benefits from a site with some shelter from strong afternoon sun, which can bleach and brown open flowers. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly after flowering only to shape, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.

common_name: Honey 'n Pearl Sweet Corn (AAS-Winning Bicolor Supersweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65F; Honey 'n Pearl is a supersweet (sh2) bicolor corn, an early landmark AAS winner bred to hold its sweetness in storage far longer than standard sweet corn.

directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows (rather than one or two long rows) for reliable wind pollination, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, after the soil has warmed to at least 65F. Honey 'n Pearl is an AAS-winning bicolor supersweet (sh2, shrunken-2 gene) corn, one of the landmark early supersweet varieties that changed home and commercial sweet corn breeding by holding its sugar content — and therefore its sweet flavor — for up to two weeks after harvest, far longer than older standard-sugary sweet corn varieties that begin converting sugar to starch within hours of picking. Ears are well-filled with a classic mix of yellow and white kernels. Because supersweet corn types can cross-pollinate badly with standard or sugary-enhanced corn and lose their sweetness, isolate plantings from other corn varieties by distance or timing. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during silking and ear fill, and side-dress with nitrogen when plants are about knee-high for the best ear development.
sources: All-America Selections — Honey 'n Pearl Sweet Corn winner announcement

planting.note: Direct sow 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 65F, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early; Sarah's Choice was bred by Dr. Brent Loy at the University of New Hampshire for unusually high sugar content and resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4-5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Sarah's Choice is a widely respected muskmelon bred by Dr. Brent Loy's public breeding program at the University of New Hampshire, selected for unusually high sugar content — commonly 14-15% Brix, well above many commercial cantaloupe varieties — along with resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt, two of the most common disease problems that shorten the productive life of melon vines. The medium-sized, heavily netted fruit has firm, deep-orange, aromatic flesh with excellent flavor. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars further. Ripe melons develop a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure — the classic 'full slip' sign of peak ripeness. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause fruit to split.
sources: University of New Hampshire — Brent Loy Cucurbit Breeding Program
